text: Alice and Bob play with piles of stones in a row. There's an even number of piles, and the total is odd, so there are no ties. They alternate turns, Alice first; each turn you take the whole pile from either the left or the right end. Both play optimally. Return true if Alice wins.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a move only ever takes from the two ends, never the middle; optimally means each player maximizes their own final total; and I return a boolean, not the score margin?
All correct. The piles array has up to five hundred entries.

Let me run through an example. Five, three, four, five gives true. Alice can grab a five from either end. The interesting part is that taking the bigger end greedily isn't always right, because it can hand the opponent a better position. So this needs game-theory DP, not greed.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive framing is a table indexed by i, j, and whose turn it is, tracking two separate scores. But there's a cleaner trick. This problem reminds me of interval DP: the state is a subarray from i to j, and every move shrinks it from one end. Then I track the score difference, not two scores. Define dp of i, j as the net score — current player minus opponent — that the player to move can guarantee on that range. The game is symmetric, so this doesn't depend on who is moving. The player dimension disappears, and I'm back to a two-D table.
Write the recurrence, and be explicit about the sign.

dp of i, j is the max of two options: take the left pile, piles of i minus dp of i plus one, j; or take the right pile, piles of j minus dp of i, j minus one. The base case is one pile: dp of i, i is just that pile. And the minus is the whole point. After I take a pile, my opponent becomes the player to move on what's left, so that smaller dp is their net advantage — and their gain is my loss. If I wrote a plus, I'd be modeling two players cooperating, which is the wrong game entirely. The answer is dp of zero, n minus one, greater than zero — Alice nets positive.

Here's the plan. One: seed the diagonal — dp of i, i equals piles of i. Two: fill by interval length, from two up to n, not by raw i and j, because each cell needs the two shorter intervals beside it. Three: return whether dp of zero, n minus one is positive. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I build an n by n table, set the diagonal, then loop the length L from two to n, and for each start i set j to i plus L minus one and take the max of left minus and right minus. One thing worth flagging — the outer loop has to be the length. A plain double loop over i and j would read dp of i plus one, j before it's filled. The inner bound, i plus L minus one below n, keeps j inside the array. That's quadratic time and quadratic space; I could roll it down to linear by keeping one diagonal, but at five hundred it's already tiny.
Is there anything special about an even number of piles and an odd total?

Yes — actually those two constraints make the answer always true, and there's a short proof. Split the piles into even-indexed and odd-indexed groups. Since the count is even, the two ends always have opposite parity. Alice can commit to taking only even-indexed piles, or only odd ones — whatever Bob takes, the pile he exposes keeps her parity available. So she can guarantee the entire even group or the entire odd group, her choice. The two groups sum to an odd total, so they can't be equal — she picks the larger one and wins. So return true is technically correct here. But I'd still submit the DP. The moment the problem relaxes — any pile count and ties allowed, or a different scoring rule — the parity trick collapses and only the interval DP survives. I'd mention the shortcut as an observation, not lean on it.

Let's dry-run five, three, four, five, filling by length — expected true. The cell that decides it is the last one, dp of zero, three. Taking the left five leaves dp of one, three, which is four; taking the right five leaves dp of zero, two, also four. So it's five minus four either way — one, greater than zero, so true. Cross-check with the parity shortcut: even indices sum to nine, odd ones to eight, and that margin of one is exactly dp of zero, three. That matches.

The DP is quadratic time and space; the shortcut is constant. Oh, one more thing — the score-difference framing is really a reusable template for two-player take-from-the-ends games. If ties are allowed, it's the same code with the answer relaxed to greater than or equal to zero. If a move scores the sum of what remains instead of the pile taken, it keeps the exact skeleton, and you get that sum in constant time from a prefix-sum array. The invariant across all of them is that single minus sign encoding now it's the opponent's turn.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You collapsed the player dimension with the score-difference trick and justified the minus sign precisely. You filled by interval length for the right dependency order. And you knew the parity shortcut existed but chose the DP because it generalizes — that's exactly the judgment I want. Strong hire.
